title: Storing water for an emergency: how much, and where else to find it
asks: how much water should i store for an emergency
how many gallons of water per person per day
how to store water for emergencies
can i store tap water for an emergency
emergency water supply for how many days
what containers do i store drinking water in
where can i find water in my house if the taps stop
how much water does my family need for two weeks
how much watter to store per person
water is out, what can we drink in the house, over
answer: FEMA: keep one gallon of drinking water per person, per day. Depending on where you live, you may wish to keep 3, 7 or even 14 days of water on hand.

Needs rise in hot weather. The Army field sanitation manual says a soldier doing normal duties in a hot and dry climate may require as much as two to six gallons of water per day for drinking, and in a cooler climate only one-half to one gallon for the same level of exertion.
Store commercially bottled water with your kit, not tap water.

Do not store bottled water in direct sunlight: the light and warmth support bacterial growth in the water. Store it in a shaded, well-ventilated area, in boxes that keep the caps elevated, and use the oldest water first.
Commercially bottled water usually has a labeled shelf life of 1 year or more.
Add extra water for your pet.
Store emergency supplies in different places, such as your home, office and vehicle. A work kit should include water, and a car kit bottled water.
Check your needs every six months.
A water purification system is on FEMA's list of other items you may want to add to the kit.
In an emergency, use bottled water, or water you have properly prepared and stored as an emergency water supply. Bottled water is your best choice.
Water that you have boiled: let it cool naturally and store it in clean containers with covers.

Other sources of water in and around your home: melt ice cubes, or drain your hot water tank or pipes. You can also use river or lake water; it is generally better to use flowing water than still, stagnant water.
Regardless of the source, treat the water before you use it.
warnings: Do not use water with floating material in it, or water that has a dark color or a questionable odor.
After a nuclear detonation, do not consume liquids that were left uncovered outdoors and may be contaminated by fallout.

quotes.text: You should store emergency supplies in different places, such as your home, office, and vehicle. Your basic emergency supply kit should include the following: Water. Keep one gallon of drinking water, per person, per day in your kit. Depending on where you live, you may wish to keep 3, 7, or even 14 days of water on hand.

For example, a Soldier performing normal duties in a hot and dry climate may require as much as two to six gallons of water per day for drinking purposes. In a cooler climate the Soldier may require only one-half to one gallon of water per day for the same level of exertion.
Store commercially bottled water with your kit, not tap water. For more information about clean drinking water and how to sanitize water if no clean water is available, visit Ready.gov.
Other items you may want to add to your emergency supply kit: Prescription medications and glasses. Infant formula and diapers. Pet food and extra water for your pet.
Complete change of clothing, including a long-sleeved shirt, long pants, and sturdy shoes. Water purification system. Fire extinguisher.
Your work kit should include food, water, comfortable walking shoes, and other necessities like medicines.
Create an emergency supply kit for your car. Include jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, bottled water, and nonperishable snacks.

After putting together your emergency supply kits, check your needs every six months. Update your kit regularly, especially as your family’s needs change, to ensure it is ready and safe when disaster strikes.

Bottled and packaged field water should not be stored in direct sunlight because the light and warmth support bacterial growth in the water. Bottles and packages of water should be stored in shaded, well-ventilated areas and in boxes which keep the caps elevated. Stored bottled/packaged field water should be used on a first in, first out basis, to keep the holding time as short as possible.
Commercially bottled water usually has a labeled shelf life of 1 year or more.
Use bottled water or water you have properly prepared and stored as an emergency water supply.
Let water cool naturally and store it in clean containers with covers.

Look for other sources of water in and around your home. Although bottled water is your best choice, you may be able to find other sources of water by melting ice cubes or draining your hot water tank or pipes. You can also use river or lake water. It is generally better to use flowing water than still, stagnant water. However, do not use water with floating material in it or water that has a dark color or questionable odor. Regardless of the source, treat the water by following the instructions on the main page above.
Do not consume food or liquids that were left uncovered outdoors and may be contaminated by fallout.

conflict: (1) Amount: FEMA P-2064 (2020) says 'one gallon of drinking water, per person, per day'. ATP 4-25.12 says a soldier doing normal duties in a hot and dry climate 'may require as much as two to six gallons of water per day for drinking purposes' (and elsewhere 'Three gallons or 12-quarts per day in hot, dry climates'), and one-half to one gallon in a cooler climate; ATP 3-50.21 says 2 to 3 quarts a day at 68 F with limited physical activity. The card shows FEMA's figure and the Army range. (2) Tap water: FEMA says 'Store commercially bottled water with your kit, not tap water'; EPA (2026) allows 'water you have properly prepared and stored as an emergency water supply' and refers to FEMA for how. No kit document explains how to prepare tap water for long storage.

review.notes: Pass. Drafter flag verdict (1 vs 2-6 gal/day): correctly shown attributed with its context (FEMA's civilian storage figure; ATP 4-25.12 'a Soldier performing normal duties in a hot and dry climate', with the cooler-climate half to one gallon); keep. The conflict field could also list ORNL-5037 (long shelter stays): 'four or five quarts of drinking water per day are essential in very hot weather' and '15 gallons per person' for a two-week stay. All other lines verified: bottled not tap (FEMA), no direct sunlight, shaded and ventilated, caps elevated, oldest first (TB MED 577, military packaged water but applicable), 1-year shelf life, pets, kits at home/work/car, six-month check, purification system, EPA emergency supply and cooled boiled water, ice cubes/hot water tank/pipes/river or lake, treat regardless of source, floating material/dark colour/odour, fallout-exposed liquids. The tap-water ask gets FEMA's 'not tap water' plus EPA's 'properly prepared and stored', and the conflict field honestly notes that no kit document explains the preparation.
